Camakapraśna
------------------------------------------
The Camakapraśna is, if we can use the expression, a ‘twin’ of the Rudrapraśna (See RUDRAPRAŚNA.). The two always go together, especially in Vedic rituals.
It occurs in the 4th kāṇḍa (book) of the 7th prapāṭhaka (section) of the Taittirīya Saṁhitā.
In culmination of the Vedic rites described in the six earlier prapāṭhakas, आज्य (ghee) has to be poured in a ladle made of audumbara wood (Ficus glomerata)—the common fig tree—in a continuous stream, technically called ‘vasor- dhārā’ (same as पूर्णाहुति in homas). For this purpose the entire Camaka (in eleven anuvākas or mantras) has to be used.
The term Camaka has been used for this piece since the words ‘ca me’ (‘and for me’) occur repeatedly.
The whole मन्त्र is a prayer addressed to God requesting him to grant the various objects of life (347 in number!) here and now which will make a man happy and be useful in यज्ञ or sacrifice.
The following are some of the objects of desire asked for: ड़ोओद्; health and strength of body; eminence and fame; balance of मिन्द्; wealth; love and good-will towards the world; ड़ोओद् and drink to maintain the body in good condition; plenty of ड़ोओद् materials; earth and its treasures; favour of Vedic gods, especially of इन्द्र; various implements of sacrifice; the facility to conduct वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
The tenth अनुवाक is a great dedicatory prayer.
The last अनुवाक ends by asking for never-ending ड़ोओद्, sacrifices to be performed, sun and rains and a prayer to the all-pervading God.

cāmara
(‘of the animal camarī’)
------------------------------------------
‘Camarī-mṛga’ is the animal yak normally found in Tibet. A long chowrie prepared from the hairs on the bushy tail of the yak was commonly used by the attendants of a king as a sort of a fan, to ward off flies and insects. However, in course of time, it became a part of the royal insignia, along with the chatra or umbrella. It is used in the ceremonial worship of a deity also, at the time of ārati or vespers.
Cāmara, according to the देवी-māhātmya section of the मार्कण्डेय Purāṇa, was one of the generals of the demon king महिषासुर, who was slain by दुर्गा.

camasa
(‘that in which [something] is partaken’)
------------------------------------------
Out of the several implements used in a Vedic sacrifice, ‘camasa’ is an important one. It is a kind of cup, with or without a handle, usually square in shape and made of the nyagrodha wood (Ficus indica). The handle could be round, square or even triangular.
It is generally used for containing the सोम juice for libation, for drinking the same by priests, and for bringing the ‘praṇītā’ waters for making dough for the चरु in a sacrifice. (See PRAṆĪTĀ.)
Out of the sixteen priests involved in a sacrifice, only ten are entitled to have चमस and they are called ‘camasins’.
The बृहदारण्यक उपनिषद् (
) compares the human head to a चमस, kept inverted.

Cāmuṇḍā
------------------------------------------
Mother worship and मोथेर् cult are not alien to Vedic religion as some suggest. The concept of अदिति (mother of gods and a personification of nature) as also the Ambhṛṇīsūkta and the रात्रिसूक्त of the ऋग्वेद clearly contain the origins of the worship of God as शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्.
One of the early basic texts of the शक्ति cult is the देवीमाहात्म्य also called दुर्गासप्तशती or चण्डी. According to this, Kālī, one of the aspects of दुर्गा that emanated from her forehead, killed the two demons Caṇḍa and मुण्ड, gene-rals of the demon king Śumbha, and got this name. She is described as a fierce goddess, black in colour, emaciated and wearing the cheetah skin as also severed human heads. Her mouth and tongue were of immense proportions. She could kill troups of demons at one stroke and could swallow several elephants in a gulp.
Cāmuṇḍā is sometimes included in the list of ‘Saptamātṛkās’ or ‘Seven Mothers’, in the place of Nārasiṁhī.
She actually symbolizes the power of time in its all-destroying aspect.
The word is also spelt as Cāmuṇḍī.
See also DURGĀ, KĀLĪ and SAPTA-MĀTṚKĀS.

Campā
------------------------------------------
Campā, variously known as चम्पा-पुरी, Campakāvatī, Campānagara and so on, was the capital of the once well-known Aṅgadeśa. रोमपाद, ड़थेर् of Śāntā and ड़थेर्-in-law of the famous sage Ṛṣya-śṛṅga, was the king here in very ancient times. रामायण mentions it. During the times of the महाभारत कर्ण was ruling from here.
It has been identified with Nathnagar near Bhagalpur in Bihar.
Some scholars opine that the famous Buddhist work, the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra was composed here probably in the 4th century A.D.
Campā is said to be the birthplace of Vāsupūjya, the twelfth Tīrthaṅkara and also associated with the last, महावीर.
Hindu religion, culture and way of life had spread beyond the borders of India even from the ancient days. There are archaeological, epigraphical and other evidences to prove its existence in the South East Asian countries from the 1st century A.D. The kingdom of Campā—the South Annam region of Vietnam—is a country of this group.
One Śrīmāra established a Hindu dynasty there in A.
. The kingdom itself—though the rulers changed now and then—continued till A.

when it was annexed by the kings of Annam.
Among the several distinguished rulers of चम्पा, the names of Bhadravarma, Rudravarma, Harivarma, महेन्द्र-varma, Jayasiṁhavarma and जय इन्द्र-varma may be mentioned. They were all Hindu rulers and had adopted Hindu ways of administration. Most of them were well-versed in Sanskrit and Hindu sciences, both religious and secular. Hence they had adopted Sanskrit as the State language.
In the social fabric, the वर्ण-आश्रम system had been deeply rooted. The various सṁस्कारस् (religio-social sacraments) like मर्रिअगे, were being done by the priests according to the Hindu धर्म-śāstras.
Though शैविस्म् had been patronized by the State, वैष्णविस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् also flourished. Several हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् including innumerable images of शिव as also liṅgas, have been discovered. However, these temples are smaller in size and are built mostly in brick. In architectural style they resemble the ‘rathas’ of महाबलिपुरम् or the temples of बादामि in Karnataka.
